contents:
Bond amounts and payments

## What is a bond?

A bond is a payment that rental providers (landlords) can request from renters at the start of a rental agreement (lease). It acts as financial protection for the rental provider and can be used to cover some costs they may have to pay when the renter moves out. Bonds are held in trust by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA), a statutory authority within the Department of Government Services.

Any renter who signs a residential rental agreement can be asked to pay a bond.

The bond is repaid at the end of the rental agreement once the rental provider and renter(s) agree on how it should be repaid. The bond is the renter’s money and should be repaid to the renter in most circumstances.

Eligible renters can also choose to port (transfer) their existing bond money to a new rental property instead of seeking a repayment. This means the renter does not need to pay a new bond while waiting for their existing bond to be repaid. To learn more, visit Portable rental bonds.

The bond and rent are separate payments. The bond cannot be used to pay rent.

If a bond has been paid, the rental provider must complete a condition report and give the renter(s) a copy before they move in.

If you are subletting, your head renter may ask you to pay a bond. Read more about subletting.

Additional information is available about lodging and claiming bonds, bond increases, and getting help if you cannot pay a bond.

Bond amounts and payments

## Maximum bond amounts

In most cases, a bond can't be more than one month’s rent.

A rental provider can only ask for a higher bond when either:

- the weekly rent for the property is more than $900
- VCAT has set a higher bond for the property. They might do this because of the character of the property or the quality of the fittings and furniture

There is no rule about maximum bond in these cases.

Different rules about bonds apply for residents of rooming houses, caravan parks and residential parks.

> **Note:** If your bond lodgement exceeds the weekly rent amount, you will receive a warning notification when you complete your lodgement. This includes if you have rounded a number. You can proceed if you believe you comply with the requirements.

Bond amounts and payments

### Maximum bond amount for rooming house residents

For residents in rooming houses, the maximum amount of bond depends on the type of agreement they have:

- The bond can't be more than 28 days’ rent for residents on a fixed-term rooming house agreement
- The bond can't be more than 14 days’ rent for residents who aren't on fixed-term agreements

A rooming house is a property where four or more people can occupy the rooms. Each resident has an individual agreement with the rooming house operator. This makes it different from a share house, where everyone signs the same agreement.

Find out more about rooming house agreements.

Bond amounts and payments

### Maximum bond amount for caravan park residents

The bond can't be more than one month’s rent or hiring charge in a caravan park.

A park owner can't ask for a bond unless the parties have a written residency agreement.

Someone renting a caravan and a site separately may have to pay two separate bonds: one for the caravan and another for the site.

Find out more about residency in a caravan park.

Bond amounts and payments

### Maximum bond amount for Part 4A park residents

A site tenant is someone who owns a moveable dwelling and rents a site in the caravan park or residential park where they live. A moveable dwelling is also called a manufactured home or relocatable home.

The bond for site tenants can't be more than the equivalent of one month’s rent if the rent is $900 a week or less.

Find out more about site agreements in residential parks and villages.

Bond amounts and payments

## How and when bonds are paid

Bonds are not mandatory. However, if a bond is requested in the rental agreement, the renter must pay it. If the bond is not paid, the rental provider can give the renter a notice to vacate.

Most rental providers ask for bonds before renters move in.

Renters can pay the bond by:

- paying the rental provider, who then pays the amount to the RTBA during the bond lodgement
- paying the RTBA directly during the bond lodgement
- using the Portable Rental Bond Scheme to transfer their existing bond money to a new rental property, if eligible

The rental provider chooses the payment method when lodging the bond. Renters should ask the rental provider to select a payment method that suits them.

Read more about different bond lodgement types.

There are rules about what happens after the renter has paid the bond:

- If the renter paid the rental provider, the rental provider must lodge the bond with the RTBA within 14 days, not including public holidays, of receiving the bond amount.
- The RTBA must give a receipt containing the bond number and other key information to the rental provider and all renters within 7 days of receiving the bond.

Once a bond has been paid, the rental provider must complete a condition report. Find out more about condition reports or lodging the bond, including how to check that the bond has been lodged.

Bond amounts and payments

## If there are multiple renters

If the renters are paying the RTBA directly, all renters will receive a link to pay. However, only one renter can pay the bond in full because it must be lodged as a single payment.

All renters should agree who will make the payment and how that renter will be reimbursed before lodging the bond.

Bond amounts and payments

## Homes Victoria bond loans

Government bond loans are available to people on low incomes who may be unable to pay a bond and have no other financial options. These are called Homes Victoria bond loans or RentAssist bond loans.

Read more about Homes Victoria bond loans.

Bond amounts and payments

## When extra bond can be requested

In most circumstances, renters will only pay a single bond for the duration of their rental agreement. A rental provider can only charge an additional bond in specific circumstances.

Rental providers can only ask for an extra bond:

- in a long-term rental agreement of more than five years, with an end date at least five years in the future
- when renters make certain changes to a property, with an agreement that the rental provider is responsible for removing those changes at the end of the lease

The rental provider must make sure they give enough notice.

The renter can challenge an extra bond request at VCAT. Among the factors it considers, VCAT will consider whether paying the extra bond would cause severe hardship for the renter.

Read the full conditions that apply to extra bonds.

Bond amounts and payments

## Relevant legislation

For the law concerning bond amounts and payments, see these sections of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*:

- Part 2, Division 2 – Bonds
- Part 10 – Bonds and the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority

Condition reports

## What is a condition report?

A condition report is a record of a property’s condition at the start of a rental agreement. Rental agreements include those for:

- rooming houses
- caravan parks
- caravans
- Part 4A sites

Anything that is unclean, damaged or not working should be included in the condition report. The report should cover the property, room or caravan, including:

- its fittings and fixtures
- everything inside and outside

All rental properties, rooming houses, caravans, caravan sites and Part 4A park sites must have condition reports.

> **Terminology note:**
>
> - ‘Rental provider’ includes landlords, rooming house operators, caravan park owners, caravan owners and Part 4A site owners.
> - ‘Renter’ includes renters, rooming house residents, park residents and site tenants.

The rental provider, or their agent, prepares the condition report. They must sign it and give two copies to the renter, or one copy if sending it electronically, before the renter moves in.

Condition reports

### Why is the condition report important?

Condition reports can be important evidence if there is a dispute about bond claims or who should pay for cleaning or repairing damage.

Condition reports

## Condition reports at the start of the agreement

The rental provider is responsible for providing two copies of the signed condition report, or one electronic copy, to the renter before they move in. The report must be created using the Condition report template (Word, 187KB). It can be provided on paper or electronically, such as by email.

The renter should check the report. If anything is inaccurate, they can change it and add their own comments. The renter should send a signed copy to the rental provider or agent and keep one for themselves.

The renter must return the report within five business days of moving into the property. Business days do not include weekends or public holidays. The renter should allow enough time for delivery if sending it by post.

If a renter is not given a condition report before moving in, they can complete their own. They should give it to the rental provider or agent within five business days of moving in.

Both the renter and rental provider should take photographs of the property at the start of the rental agreement, particularly if there is pre-existing damage.

Photographs should be dated, labelled and attached to the condition report. They can be kept as hard copies or digital files.

A condition report that records something requiring repair gives the rental provider written notice of the issue. If the repairs are not completed within a reasonable period, the renter can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs to be completed.

The rental provider or agent and the renter must keep a copy of the condition report until the rental agreement ends.

Condition reports

### Report an issue with an advertised rental property

Prospective renters, real estate agents or members of the public who have concerns about an advertised rental property can report an issue with an advertised rental property to Consumer Affairs Victoria.

Condition reports

### Disputes about the condition report

It is best for the renter and rental provider to work together to resolve disagreements about the condition report.

If the renter or rental provider believes the condition report is incorrect or incomplete, either party can apply to VCAT for a decision. They must apply within 30 days of the start of the rental agreement.

Condition reports

## Condition reports at the end of the agreement

When a rental agreement ends, the rental provider or agent must complete the ‘Exit condition report’ section of the original condition report within 10 days.

The renter must be present when this happens or must have been given a reasonable opportunity to be present. Reasonable means what most people would consider fair.

The exit condition report records the condition of the property at the end of the tenancy.

Condition reports

## Claiming the bond using the condition report

A rental provider or agent may be able to use the condition report to claim part or all of the bond at the end of a rental agreement if:

- there is new damage to the property, room, hired caravan or site that is not normal wear and tear
- the property needs new repairs
- the property requires further cleaning
- items are missing

If there is a dispute about the bond, either the renter or rental provider can apply to VCAT. This process is free if the claim is for an amount less than the bond paid.

Read more about claiming the bond.

Condition reports

## Condition of the property and repairs

There are minimum standards for the condition of rental properties and rooming houses.

There are also rules concerning:

- repairs and urgent repairs in rental properties and rooming houses
- responsibility for managing pests and mould
- renters installing fixtures and making changes to the property

Condition reports

## Cleaning responsibilities

Renters and residents must keep the property in a reasonably clean condition.

When moving out, renters and residents must leave the property:

- reasonably clean
- in the same condition as when they moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear

For rental agreements signed from 29 March 2021, additional requirements apply to professional cleaning. Rental providers cannot require renters to arrange professional cleaning unless the property:

- needs to be returned to the condition it was in at the start of the rental agreement, allowing for fair wear and tear; for example, if it was professionally cleaned before the renter moved in
- is in a condition that requires professional cleaning

Read more in Guideline 2 – Cleanliness (Word, 244KB).

Condition reports

## Forms you might need

Use the official template to create a condition report:

- Condition report template (Word, 187KB)

Condition reports

## Relevant legislation

Condition reports are covered by these sections of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*:

- Section 35
- Section 97
- Section 148
- Section 206O

Rental properties - minimum standards

# Rental properties—minimum standards

From 25 November 2025, rental properties must meet the minimum standards before they are advertised.

From 1 December 2025, cords on internal window coverings must be secured to prevent them from forming loops.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## Rental properties must meet the minimum standards

There are 15 categories of minimum standards for rental properties. Every rental property must comply with the requirements in each applicable category.

Rental providers and agents must ensure that a property meets the minimum standards:

- when the property is advertised or offered for rent
- before the renter moves into the property.

The detailed requirements are provided in the 15 categories of minimum standards section of this document.

Different requirements apply to minimum standards in rooming houses.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## When minimum standards apply

A rental property must meet the minimum standards before it is advertised.

For existing rental agreements, the minimum standards in Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 apply when the agreement:

- started on or after 29 March 2021
- started before 29 March 2021 but became a periodic, or month-to-month, agreement on or after 29 March 2021.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## When minimum standards do not apply

The minimum standards do not apply to an agreement that became a periodic, or month-to-month, agreement before 29 March 2021.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## Renters’ rights when minimum standards are not met

Renters have rights when a property does not comply with the minimum standards, including when the rental provider fails to complete the required repairs.

See renters’ rights when minimum standards are not met.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Checklist for rental providers

Rental providers should review the minimum standards before allowing a renter to move into a rental property.

Download the Rental minimum standards checklist for rental providers (PDF, 160 KB).

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Checklist for renters

Renters should review the minimum standards before moving into a new rental property.

Download the Rental minimum standards checklist for renters (PDF, 152 KB).

Rental properties - minimum standards

## Minimum-standard categories

New minimum rental standards for energy efficiency will take effect from 1 March 2027. See new minimum energy-efficiency standards.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Bathrooms

A rental property’s bathroom must have:

- a washbasin
- a shower or bath
- a reasonable supply of hot and cold water.

The shower must have a shower head with a three-star water-efficiency rating.

If a three-star shower head cannot be installed, for example because of the property’s age, a one-star or two-star shower head is acceptable.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Electrical safety

The electrical-safety minimum standard commenced on 29 March 2023.

Rental properties must have a modern switchboard containing:

- circuit breakers
- electrical safety switches.

Electrical safety switches include residual current devices known as RCDs, RCCBs or RCBOs.

The rental provider must engage an electrician to ensure the property complies with the electrical-safety standard.

#### Properties with a circuit-breaker switchboard

An electrician may add circuit-breaker components to the power-outlet and lighting circuits without modifying the protection for other circuits.

The required components may include:

- an overcurrent circuit breaker and residual current device
- an overcurrent circuit breaker and residual current-operated circuit breaker without integral overcurrent protection
- a residual current-operated circuit breaker with integral overcurrent protection.

#### Properties without a circuit-breaker switchboard

Some older properties have panel-and-fuse boards or federal fuse boards instead of circuit-breaker switchboards.

If circuit-breaker components cannot be added to the existing board, an electrician may need to replace the entire switchboard.

In this situation, circuit-breaker protection must be provided for all circuits, including:

- power outlets and lighting
- fixed cooking equipment
- hot-water units
- air-conditioning circuits.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Heating

Every rental property must have a fixed heater in good working order in the main living area. A portable heater does not satisfy this requirement.

For rental agreements entered into from 29 March 2023, the main living area must have an energy-efficient fixed heater. If an existing fixed heater is not energy efficient, the rental provider must upgrade it.

An energy-efficient fixed heater must be one of the following:

- a non-ducted air conditioner or heat pump with an energy rating of at least two stars
- a gas space heater with an energy rating of at least two stars
- a ducted or hydronic heating system with an outlet in the main living area
- a domestic solid-fuel appliance, such as a fireplace or wood-burning stove.

#### Heating requirements for apartments

Installing an energy-efficient heater may be considered unreasonable in some apartment buildings if:

- the installation cost would be significantly higher than the average installation cost in a domestic apartment building
- owners-corporation rules prohibit the installation
- another Act or local law makes the installation cost prohibitive.

Even when installing an energy-efficient heater is unreasonable, the rental provider must still install a working fixed heater in the main living area.

The rental provider should retain evidence explaining why installation of an energy-efficient heater is unreasonable and tell the renter before entering into the rental agreement.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Kitchen

The property must have a kitchen containing:

- a dedicated cooking and food-preparation area
- a working sink connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water
- a working stovetop with at least two burners.

If the property has an oven, it must be in good working order.

These requirements do not apply when the property:

- is listed on the Heritage Council Victoria register
- has an approved exemption from the standard.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Laundry

If the property has a laundry, it must be connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Lighting

Rooms, corridors and hallways must have enough light to make them functional.

During the day, natural light may be received from an adjoining room. At night, renters must have access to artificial light.

These requirements do not apply if the property is registered under the *Heritage Act 2017* and has an approved exemption.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Locks

External entry doors must have:

- functioning deadlocks
- or locks that require a key to unlock from outside but can be unlocked without a key from inside.

A deadlock is a deadlatch containing at least one cylinder.

A deadlock is not required when:

- the door cannot be secured with a deadlock because of its position
- it is a screen door in the same frame as an external door
- another Act or law requires a different lock or security device
- another security barrier prevents access to the door, such as a locked apartment-building entrance or gate
- the property is registered under the *Heritage Act 2017* and has an approved exemption.

See locks and security.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Mould and damp

All rooms must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Structural soundness

The property must be:

- structurally sound
- weatherproof.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Toilets

The toilet must be in good working order and connected to:

- a reticulated sewerage system
- a wastewater-treatment system permitted under EPA Victoria’s onsite wastewater-management requirements
- another system approved by the local council.

The toilet must be located in a separate room, either:

- by itself
- in a bathroom
- in a combined bathroom and laundry.

See EPA Victoria and Victorian local councils for relevant requirements.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Ventilation

The property must have adequate ventilation in all habitable rooms, including:

- bathrooms
- showers
- toilets
- laundries.

The property must satisfy the applicable ventilation requirements of the Building Code of Australia.

See the Australian Building Codes Board resource library.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Vermin-proof bins

The rental provider must supply:

- a rubbish bin
- a recycling bin.

The bins may be supplied by the local council or purchased elsewhere. They must:

- prevent access by vermin such as rats and mice
- meet local-council collection requirements.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Windows

Every external window capable of opening must have a functioning latch that secures it against external entry.

An openable window must also be capable of remaining in either an open or closed position.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Window coverings

Windows in rooms likely to be used as bedrooms or living areas must have curtains or blinds that:

- can be closed
- block light
- provide privacy.

Rental properties - minimum standards

### Window-covering anchors

From 1 December 2025, every corded internal window covering must have an anchor that secures its cords and prevents them from forming loops.

This requirement applies to corded blinds, curtains and similar internal window coverings.

Renters and rental providers can order a free curtain and blind cord-safety kit or purchase one from a hardware store.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## Regulations

Rental-property minimum standards are specified in Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021.

Requirements for window-covering anchors are addressed in the Residential Tenancies Amendment (Housing Statement Reform and Part 4A Site Agreements) Regulations.

Rental properties - minimum standards

## Sections of the Act

Rental-property minimum standards are addressed by the following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997:

- **Section 65A:** Occupation of rented premises that do not comply with rental minimum standards.
- **Section 65B:** Advertising premises that do not comply with rental minimum standards.
- **Section 72:** Urgent repairs.
- **Section 77:** Payment of rent into the Rent Special Account.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

# Notice to vacate in rental properties

Related information is available about:

- Renters giving notice
- Evictions and possession orders

Different notice rules apply to:

- Rooming-house residents
- Caravan-park residents
- Site tenants in residential parks or villages

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## What is a notice to vacate?

When a rental provider wants a renter to move out, the rental provider can:

- discuss ending the agreement with the renter and reach an agreement
- give the renter a formal notice to vacate.

A notice to vacate is a formal statement that the rental provider wants to end the rental agreement. A rental provider can only issue one for a legally valid reason.

If the renter does not leave by the termination date stated in the notice, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for an eviction or possession order.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Reasons rental providers can and cannot give notice

A rental provider must:

- give a legally valid reason for issuing a notice to vacate
- state that reason in the notice
- comply with the applicable notice period and other requirements.

A notice issued without a valid reason is not valid.

In some circumstances, a rental provider can issue a notice before the rental agreement’s stated end date.

A rental provider cannot issue a notice because a renter exercised, or said they would exercise, a legal right. For example, a notice cannot be issued because the renter:

- requested repairs
- asked for permission to keep a pet
- challenged a rent increase.

A notice to vacate is also invalid if it involves unlawful discrimination.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

### Agreement to leave without formal notice

A rental provider may ask a renter to leave without issuing a formal notice to vacate.

The renter:

- does not have to agree to leave
- should record the agreement in writing if they agree.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

### Immediate notice

A rental provider can issue an immediate notice to vacate if the renter or the renter’s visitor:

- intentionally or recklessly causes serious damage to the property, safety equipment or common areas
- puts neighbours, the rental provider, the rental provider’s agent, contractors or employees in danger.

See immediate notices.

Additional rules apply to:

- Violent or dangerous behaviour in rooming houses
- Violent or dangerous behaviour in caravan parks

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## How to give a notice to vacate

A rental provider should use the Notice to vacate to renter or renters of rented premises (Word, 760 KB).

The notice must:

- be addressed to the renter
- state the reason for ending the rental agreement
- be signed by the rental provider or their agent
- allow enough time for delivery
- state the date by which the renter must leave, known as the termination date.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

### Delivering a notice to vacate

The notice must be delivered to the renter at the rented premises using one of the following methods:

- registered post
- electronic communication, such as email, if the renter consented to receive notices electronically
- personal delivery by hand.

When sending the notice by post, the rental provider must:

- use registered post
- consider the delivery method and posting location
- allow sufficient time for delivery.

See Australia Post delivery estimates.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Challenging a notice to vacate

A renter can challenge a notice to vacate if they:

- believe it was not delivered correctly
- disagree with the reason stated in the notice
- received the notice because of family violence.

See challenging a notice to vacate.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## When a renter does not leave

If a renter does not leave after receiving a valid notice to vacate, the rental provider can apply for a possession order.

See possession orders and evictions.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## When a renter dies

If a property has only one renter and that renter dies, the rental provider can end the agreement by giving a notice to vacate to:

- the deceased renter’s legal personal representative
- the deceased renter’s next of kin.

See what happens when a renter or rental provider dies.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Ending an agreement early—reasons and notice periods

A rental provider can only end a rental agreement before its stated end date for a legally recognised reason.

A notice to vacate is invalid if the rental provider does not give one of the permitted reasons.

The minimum notice period depends on the reason for ending the agreement.

Related information includes:

- Late or unpaid rent
- Keeping pets without consent
- Not paying an agreed bond

Notice to vacate in rental properties

### Reasons for ending an agreement early

| Reason for notice to vacate | Minimum notice required |
|---|---:|
| The renter or their visitor intentionally or recklessly causes serious damage to the property, including safety equipment or common areas. | Immediate |
| The renter or their visitor puts neighbours, the rental provider, the rental provider’s agent, contractors or employees in danger. | Immediate |
| The premises are unfit for human habitation, completely destroyed or damaged to the extent that they are unsafe. | Immediate |
| The renter or another person living at the property seriously threatens or intimidates the rental provider, their agent, contractors or employees. | 14 days |
| The renter owes at least 14 days’ rent. | 14 days |
| The renter has failed to comply with a VCAT compliance order. | 14 days |
| The renter has received two breach-of-duty notices and commits the same breach again. | 14 days |
| The property is being used for illegal purposes. | 14 days |
| The renter has brought in other renters or subletters without consent. | 14 days |
| The renter has not paid the bond as agreed. | 14 days |
| The renter has a child under 16 living at the premises when the rental agreement states this is not allowed. | 14 days |
| The rental provider is a government housing authority and the renter misled the authority to obtain social housing. | 14 days |
| The renter has been involved in drug-related activity in public housing. | 14 days |
| The renter is keeping a pet without consent and VCAT has made an order excluding the pet. | 28 days |

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Notice to vacate at the end of an agreement

A rental provider cannot issue a notice to vacate at the end of a fixed-term rental agreement without a valid reason.

Generally, the minimum notice period for a valid reason is 90 days. A shorter period applies in certain circumstances.

Some reasons require supporting evidence, such as:

- a building permit
- a statutory declaration
- a contract or quotation
- evidence that a property is being sold.

If the required evidence is not included, the notice may be invalid.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

### Reasons for giving notice at the end of an agreement

For a fixed-term rental agreement:

- the termination date must be on or after the agreement’s end date
- the notice must state a valid reason.

For a periodic, or month-to-month, agreement, a rental provider can give notice at any time, but must provide a valid reason.

Some reasons require documentary evidence. If the required evidence is not provided with the notice, the notice is invalid.

#### Rental provider plans to move into the property

**Minimum notice:** 14 days.

This reason must have been included in the additional terms of the fixed-term rental agreement.

The notice must include both:

- the rental agreement showing the relevant additional term, as required by section 91ZW
- a witnessed statutory declaration from the rental provider confirming the date they intend to occupy the property.

If there is more than one rental provider, each provider must supply a statutory declaration.

#### Reconstruction, repairs or renovations

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

This reason applies when the planned work cannot be completed while the renter remains in the property and all necessary permits have been obtained.

For repairs, the notice must include both:

- photographic evidence showing that repairs are required
- a contract or quotation from a suitably qualified tradesperson.

The contract or quotation must state:

1. the nature of the required repairs
2. why the renter must vacate for the repairs to be completed
3. the estimated time required to complete the repairs.

Alternatively, the rental provider can provide a building permit for repairs or renovations.

A building permit is the only documentary evidence accepted to support a notice issued specifically for renovations.

#### Property will be demolished

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

The notice must include both:

- a building permit for demolition
- a contract with a suitably qualified builder-demolisher stating when demolition will occur.

Unless VCAT gives permission, the rental provider must not re-let the property as a residence within six months after issuing the notice.

#### Property will be used for another purpose

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

This includes situations where the rental provider intends to use the property for a business instead of as a residence.

The notice must include a witnessed statutory declaration that:

- identifies the proposed business use
- provides details of the business
- states that the property will not be re-let as a residence within six months after the notice was issued.

If there is more than one rental provider, each provider must supply a statutory declaration.

The rental provider must also provide at least one of the following:

- the business’s Australian Business Number
- business registration or licence
- a council planning permit.

#### Rental provider, family member or dependent will move in

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

This reason can apply when the intended occupant is:

- the rental provider
- a member of the rental provider’s immediate family, including a parent or parent-in-law
- a dependent who normally lives with the rental provider.

The notice must include a witnessed statutory declaration stating either:

- that the rental provider intends to occupy the property
- or the intended occupant’s name, their relationship to the rental provider and whether they are a dependent.

The declaration must also confirm that the rental provider understands that the property cannot be re-let as a residence to someone other than the named occupant within six months after the notice was issued, unless VCAT permits it.

If there is more than one rental provider, each provider must supply a statutory declaration.

#### Property will be sold or offered for sale

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

The property must be vacated immediately after the rental agreement ends. The rental provider cannot shorten the agreement to issue a notice for this reason.

The notice must include one of the following:

- a dated contract of sale signed by the vendor and purchaser
- a contract of engagement or authority to sell with a licensed estate agent
- a contract of sale prepared by a conveyancer or Australian legal practitioner.

Unless VCAT gives permission, the property must not be re-let as a residence within six months after the notice was issued.

#### Government authority requires the property for public purposes

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

The notice must include one of the following:

- publicly available acquisition details
- a compulsory acquisition letter from the government.

#### Renter no longer qualifies for social housing

**Minimum notice:** 90 days.

This reason applies when:

- the rental provider is a government housing authority
- the renter no longer meets the eligibility criteria for social housing.

No specific documentary evidence is listed on the source page.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Mortgagee giving notice to vacate

A mortgagee, such as a bank, can give the renter a notice to vacate when repossessing the property.

Specific legal requirements apply to notices issued by mortgagees. Refer to the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for further information.

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Forms

To issue a notice to vacate for a rental property, the rental provider should use the:

- Notice to vacate to renter or renters of rented premises (Word, 760 KB)

Notice to vacate in rental properties

## Sections of the Act

Notices to vacate are covered by Part 2, Division 9 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, concerning the termination of residential rental agreements.

Rent increases

# Rent increases

From 25 November 2025, the minimum notice period for rental providers to issue a rent increase notice changed from 60 days to 90 days.

Learn more about changes to Victorian rental laws.

Other relevant information includes:

- Resolving rental disputes
- Renter giving notice
- Notice to vacate in rental properties
- Late or unpaid rent

Rent increases

## Rules for increasing rent

A rental provider can increase the rent for their property, but they must follow the applicable rental laws.

A rental provider cannot increase the rent during a fixed-term rental agreement unless the agreement contains an additional term allowing an increase. If an increase is permitted, the agreement must also state how the increase will be calculated.

To increase the rent, the rental provider must give the renter a Notice of proposed rent increase (Word, 72 KB).

The notice must:

- be provided using the method agreed to in the rental agreement
- be given at least 90 days before the proposed increase takes effect
- allow additional delivery time if it is sent by post.

See Australia Post delivery time estimates when sending the notice by post.

These rules apply to:

- rented residential premises
- rooming houses
- caravan parks.

Different rules apply to rent increases under a residential park site agreement.

Rent increases

### Important information

- A rent increase may be invalid if the applicable rent-increase rules are not followed.
- Renters can challenge a rent increase if they believe it is higher than the market range.
- There are limits on how often rent can be increased.

Rent increases

## How much rent can increase

The law does not specify exactly how much a rental provider can increase the rent.

However, the rental provider must explain how the proposed increase was calculated.

A rental provider cannot increase rent during a fixed-term rental agreement unless the agreement permits it. If the agreement allows an increase, it must state how the increase will be calculated.

The rental provider must notify the renter using the Notice of rent increase form at least 90 days before the increase is due to begin.

The notice must:

- specify the amount of the rent increase
- explain the method used to calculate the increase
- calculate the increase consistently with the method stated in the notice.

Rent increases

### Common calculation methods

The four most common methods for calculating a rent increase are:

- **Consumer Price Index (CPI):** Based on general price changes reported by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
- **Rent index:** Based on average Victorian rent prices reported through the metropolitan or regional rent index.
- **Fixed percentage:** A specified percentage increase, such as 3%.
- **Fixed dollar amount:** A specified dollar increase, such as $10.

Rental providers may use another calculation method. However:

- Referring to a calculation method without explaining it is not sufficient.
- The calculation information in the rental agreement and notice must be clear.
- The renter must be able to determine how the increase was calculated.
- The renter must be able to determine whether the increase matches the rental agreement.

For example, a rental agreement may state that rent will increase by $5 every 12 months. The rental provider may therefore issue a notice increasing the rent by $5 after the required period.

Rent increases

### Examples of invalid and valid wording

These examples provide general guidance and are not an exhaustive list.

#### Invalid wording

The following wording does not explain the calculation clearly enough:

- “Rent increased by dollar amount.”
- “Based on the rental market valuation.”
- “As per rental provider’s instructions.”
- “All properties in the same building are leased between [price range].”
- “CPI.”

#### Valid wording

The following examples identify a specific increase and its calculation method:

- “The next rent increase will be by 1.8%, in line with the Consumer Price Index increase reported by the Australian Bureau of Statistics for the September 2025 quarter.”
- “The next rent increase will be by $20, in line with the statewide rent increase for the June 2025 quarter.”

If an estate agent manages the property, the agent must prepare the Notice of rent increase correctly and obtain clear instructions from the rental provider. An incorrectly prepared notice may breach the agent’s professional conduct obligations.

A renter who believes a rent increase is invalid can request a rent increase review.

Rent increases

## How often rent can increase

A rental provider can only increase rent at certain times. The permitted frequency depends on:

- the type of rental agreement
- when the agreement started
- whether the agreement allows rent increases.

In most cases, rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months, even if the rental agreement specifies an earlier increase.

Rent increases

### Fixed-term agreements of five years or less

A rental agreement with an end date is a fixed-term agreement. Most fixed-term agreements are five years or less.

The rental provider must generally wait until the agreement ends before increasing the rent unless the agreement permits an increase during the fixed term.

If the agreement permits an increase:

- For agreements that started before 19 June 2019, rent cannot be increased more than once every six months.
- For agreements that started on or after 19 June 2019, rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.
- For rooming-house, residential-park or caravan-park agreements that started after 29 March 2021, rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.

Rent increases

### Fixed-term agreements longer than five years

A fixed-term rental agreement lasting more than five years is called a long-term rental agreement. These agreements were previously called long-term leases.

Under a long-term rental agreement, rent can only be increased when:

- the agreement permits rent increases
- at least 12 months have passed since the previous increase.

Rent increases

### Periodic agreements

A periodic rental agreement does not have an end date. It is often described as a month-by-month agreement.

A fixed-term agreement usually becomes periodic automatically when it ends unless the parties enter into another fixed-term agreement.

For periodic agreements:

- If the agreement started before 19 June 2019, rent cannot be increased more than once every six months.
- If the agreement became periodic on or after 19 June 2019, rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.

These limits continue to apply even if the agreement has been periodic for several years.

After receiving a rent increase, the renter can:

- accept the increase
- request a rent assessment
- end the agreement by giving a notice of intention to vacate.

Rent increases

### Social housing

Special rent rules apply to social housing.

Social-housing rent may be based on:

- the market rental rate
- the renter’s income.

The market rate is assessed once a year, while income is assessed twice a year. A change in either assessment may change the amount of rent payable.

See market rent and fixed rent in social housing for more information.

Rent increases

## Telling renters about rent increases

A rental provider must notify the renter at least 90 days before a rent increase takes effect. They must use the appropriate Notice of proposed rent increase form.

The notice must explain:

- the amount of the rent increase
- how the increase was calculated
- what the renter can do if they believe the increase is too high.

If rent is increased during a fixed-term agreement, the agreement must state the method used to calculate the increase. Examples include:

- Consumer Price Index
- rent index
- fixed percentage
- fixed dollar amount.

Rent increases

### Required notice forms

A rent increase is not valid unless the rental provider uses the correct form.

The applicable forms are:

- Notice of proposed rent increase to renter of rented premises (Word, 85 KB)
- Notice of proposed rent increase to resident of rooming house (Word, 76 KB)
- Notice of proposed rent or hiring charge increase to residents of caravan park (Word, 82 KB)
- Notice of site rent increase—fixed amount under site agreement (Word, 70 KB)
- Notice of proposed site rent increase—non-fixed amount (Word, 82 KB)

If the rental provider does not use the correct form, the notice is invalid. The renter only has to pay the increased amount after receiving valid notice.

Rent increases

## Rent cannot be increased to penalise a renter

A rental provider cannot increase rent as a penalty because the renter has breached a term of the rental agreement.

A rental agreement must not contain a term requiring the renter to pay higher rent after breaching the agreement. A prohibited term:

- cannot be enforced
- may result in financial penalties for the rental provider.

A renter who finds such a term in their agreement should contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

See penalties under Victorian rental laws for further information.

Rent increases

## Changes to the bond when rent increases

An additional bond can only be requested when a long-term rental agreement is renewed for another fixed term of more than five years.

The rental provider must:

- give the renter 120 days’ written notice
- use the Notice requesting additional bond
- request an additional bond no more than once every five years
- lodge the additional bond with the RTBA within 10 business days after receiving it.

The renter must pay the additional bond within the 120-day notice period.

An additional bond cannot be required for:

- a periodic rental agreement
- a short-term fixed rental agreement.

Rent increases

### Calculating the additional bond

To calculate the additional bond:

1. Determine the total bond that would normally be payable for the next five years of the agreement.
2. Subtract the bond already held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority.

The renter can apply to VCAT to request:

- a change to the rental agreement preventing the rental provider from requiring an additional bond
- a change to the amount of additional bond payable.

Rent increases

## Forms

The official forms for notifying renters and residents about rent increases are listed in the Required notice forms section of this document.

The correct form must be selected for the relevant accommodation type:

- rented residential premises
- rooming houses
- caravan parks
- fixed-amount site agreements
- non-fixed-amount site agreements.

Rent increases are covered by the following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997:

- **Section 44:** Rent increases under residential rental agreements.
- **Section 101:** Required notice of a rent increase for a rooming house.

Rent payments and rent in advance

# Rent payments and rent in advance

A rental agreement (lease) must state how much the rent is and how often it must be paid.

Rent must be paid to the rental provider, who may be an agent, an owner, a site owner or an operator of a rooming house or caravan park.

Renters must pay rent according to the rental agreement.

There are rules about requesting and accepting rent in advance, providing receipts and requesting additional fee payments from renters.

Related information is available about:

- late or unpaid rent
- rent increases
- challenging a rent increase

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Methods of payment

The renter and rental provider should agree on how rent will be paid before starting the rental agreement.

Before they agree, the rental provider must tell the renter about any costs associated with the selected payment method.

The rental provider must:

- provide at least one payment method that does not require the renter to pay a fee, other than the renter’s own bank fees
- allow rent to be paid through the Commonwealth Centrepay bill-paying service and another form of electronic funds transfer
- make the renter aware of any fees that may result from using the agreed payment method, such as dishonour fees
- not require the renter to pay using a post-dated cheque

Neither the renter nor the rental provider can ask the other to reimburse the costs of:

- setting up accounts to make or receive rental payments
- expenses associated with making or receiving payments, such as bank fees

Any change to how rent is paid must be agreed upon by the renter and rental provider.

Rent payments and rent in advance

### Rental provider

Rental providers cannot charge fees or fines for:

- issuing a rent payment card
- establishing or using direct debit facilities
- processing rent payments
- late payment of rent

Rental providers cannot include clauses in rental agreements requiring these fines or fees to be paid. Such clauses are illegal.

Rent payments and rent in advance

### Third-party businesses

Rental providers and agents may use a third-party platform to manage a renter’s rental agreement and rent payments.

If a renter pays rent or applies for a rental property through a third-party platform, the business operating that platform must not charge the renter a fee.

> **Note:** This restriction does not include the renter’s standard bank fees.

Rent payments and rent in advance

## How often and when to pay

The rental agreement states whether rent will be paid weekly, fortnightly, monthly or at another agreed interval.

Once the rental agreement starts, rent is due on the agreed date using the agreed payment method.

Renters paying by electronic funds transfer should allow at least 24 hours for the payment to reach the rental provider’s account. For example, the renter can transfer the rent one day before the due date to avoid the payment being considered late.

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Charging rent in advance

When a renter starts a rental agreement, they are usually required to pay rent in advance before moving into the property.

A rental provider cannot ask for or accept more than one month’s rent in advance unless:

- rent is paid weekly, in which case the rental provider can only request 14 days’ rent in advance
- rent is more than $900 per week, in which case the advance payment may be up to the full value of the rental agreement

Rent payments and rent in advance

### Rent in advance in rooming houses, caravan parks and residential parks and villages

Special rules apply to rooming houses, caravan parks, residential parks and villages with Part 4A site agreements. Read more about properties covered by Part 4A site agreements.

The advance-payment limits are:

- rooming house operators cannot charge more than 14 days’ rent in advance
- caravan park owners cannot charge more than 14 days’ rent in advance for site rental
- caravan owners cannot charge more than 28 days’ hiring charge in advance for caravan rental
- Part 4A site owners cannot charge more than one month’s rent in advance

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Stopping rent payments

Renters must not stop paying rent until they have agreed with the rental provider on a date to stop.

Renters must continue paying rent even if:

- the rental provider or owner refuses to complete repairs
- it is the final month of the rental agreement
- the renter has given notice to end the rental agreement and leave the property
- the renter has received a notice to vacate

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Providing rent receipts

Rental providers or their agents must provide renters with receipts for rent payments:

- immediately when rent is paid in person
- within five business days after receiving a request

Rental providers must keep rent-payment records for at least 12 months.

A rent receipt must contain:

- the rental provider’s name and signature
- the property address
- the payment date
- the period covered by the payment
- the amount paid
- a clear statement that the document is a rent receipt

Rental providers can be fined for failing to follow the rent-receipt requirements.

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Overpaid rent

Rent under a residential rental agreement generally accrues from day to day. Overpaid rent is recoverable or refundable on that basis.

Rent payments and rent in advance

## Relevant legislation

The rules concerning rent payments and rent in advance are covered by these sections of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*:

- Sections 39–49 – Rents for residential rental agreements
- Section 51A – Prohibited rental and application fees
- Sections 99–107 – Rent for rooming houses
- Sections 150–160 – Rent and hiring charges for caravan parks
- Sections 206S–206ZC – Rent and other charges for Part 4A sites

Repairs in rental properties

# Repairs in rental properties

Repairs are either ‘urgent’ or ‘non-urgent’. Rental providers must make urgent repairs immediately. Rental providers must make non-urgent repairs within 14 days of getting a written request.

There are rules for what happens if a rental provider ignores a request for a repair to be made.

Renters must continue to pay rent even if they are waiting for a repair to be made.

Repairs in rental properties

## Scope of this information

This information about repairs applies to rental properties, rooming houses, caravan parks and residential parks. For ease of reading, the term ‘rental provider’ includes a rooming house operator, caravan owner and caravan park operator. The term ‘renter’ includes renters and residents.

For other information about repairs, see:

- Repairs under a park site agreement
- Repairs to communal park facilities
- Resolving rental disputes

Repairs in rental properties

## The difference between urgent and non-urgent repairs

The law defines a list of urgent repairs. Anything else is a non-urgent repair. A repair is non-urgent if the renter can continue to safely live in the property. Non-urgent repairs include things like a broken dishwasher or loose bathroom tiles.
If a repair is not on the list, it is a non-urgent or general repair.

Repairs in rental properties

## List of urgent repairs

Urgent repairs must be done immediately because they make the property unsafe or difficult to live in.

Anything on this list is legally defined as an urgent repair:
- burst water service
- blocked or broken toilet system
- serious roof leak
- gas leak
- dangerous electrical fault
- flooding or serious flood damage
- serious storm or fire damage
- an essential service or appliance for hot water, water, cooking, heating, or laundering is not working
- the gas, electricity or water supply is not working
- a cooling appliance or service provided by the rental provider is not working
- the property does not meet minimum standards
- a safety-related device, such as a smoke alarm or pool fence, is not working
- an appliance, fitting or fixture that is not working and causes a lot of water to be wasted
- any fault or damage in the property that makes it unsafe or insecure, including pests, mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure
- a serious problem with a lift or staircase.

Repairs in rental properties

## Organising and paying for repairs

The rental provider must organise and pay for all repairs if they are not the renter’s fault.

If the renter caused the damage, the renter may have to pay for the repairs.

Renters must tell their rental provider or property manager in writing about any repairs that need to be made as soon as possible.

Repairs in rental properties

### Urgent repairs

Renters must contact the rental provider or agent straight away to ask for an urgent repair to be made.

Renters should:

- use the emergency phone number they were given when they moved in to contact the provider
- confirm their request in writing in case they need to prove they made the request

Rental providers or agents must make sure the repair is done immediately.

If the rental provider or agent does not respond to the request, the renter can organise and pay for the repair. They can only do this if the repair does not cost more than $2500. The rental provider must pay them back within 7 days. If the funds are not reimbursed within 7 days, the renter can apply to Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV) for help.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT for a compensation order.

Renters who cannot afford to pay $2500 upfront can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria using the online enquiries form.

Repairs in rental properties

### Non-urgent repairs

A request for general repairs should:

- be in writing
- include the date on the request

Consumer Affairs Victoria recommends using one of these forms to request a non-urgent repair:

- Renters: Notice to rental provider of rented premises (Word, 97KB)
- Caravan park residents: Notice to owner of caravan or caravan park (Word, 743KB)
- Rooming house residents: Notice to operator of rooming house (Word, 734KB)

Rental providers or agents must make sure the repair is done within 14 days from the date of the request. Renters can take steps if rental providers are not responding.

Repairs in rental properties

## Who can make a repair

For work that requires a license or registration, the renter or rental provider must use a qualified person.

All repairs must be made to the standard a tradesperson would make them.

A renter or rental provider can make a repair (that doesn't require a licence or registration) as long as they do it to the same standard as a tradesperson.

Repairs in rental properties

## Paying rent during repairs

Renters must continue to pay rent while waiting for repairs to be done or waiting to be paid back for repairs. However, they can apply to RDRV for their rent to be paid into CAV’s Rent Special Account. This means CAV holds the rent and the rental provider does not receive it until the issue is sorted out.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT

Repairs in rental properties

## Rental provider does not respond to a request

Renters should keep a record of their attempts to contact their rental provider.

If your rental provider or agent has not organised a timely repair, the renter can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria through the online enquiries form.

Repairs in rental properties

### Urgent repairs costing $2500 or less

Renters can organise and pay for urgent repairs themselves when:

- they have notified the rental provider or property manager
- there has not been a prompt response
- the urgent repair costs $2500 or less.

 Renters should keep all receipts and give the landlord a written notice asking them to repay the cost of the urgent repairs.

They must do this within 7 days of the repairs being made.

Rental providers have 7 days to pay from the date they receive written notice. If the rental provider does not repay, the renter can apply to RDRV.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT. VCAT can order the rental provider to repay the renter.

#### Forms for requesting repayment

The following forms can be used to notify a rental provider about payment for an urgent repair:

- Renters: Notice to rental provider of rented premises (Word, 97KB)
- Caravan park residents: Notice to owner of caravan or caravan park (Word, 743KB)
- Rooming house residents: Notice to operator of rooming house (Word, 734KB)

Repairs in rental properties

### Urgent repairs costing more than $2500

Renters cannot organise and pay for urgent repairs that cost more than $2500. Instead, they should apply to RDRV for help. RDRV will review the application within two business days.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT for a repair order. VCAT can order the rental provider to arrange and pay for the repairs

Repairs in rental properties

### Non-urgent repairs

Renters have rights if the rental provider does not make non-urgent repairs within 14 days of the date of the written request.  

Renters can ask us to do a repairs inspection so they can get a report directing the rental provider to make the repairs. If the report says the rental provider has to make the repairs but they are still not done, the renter can ask RDRV for help to enforce the report.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT.

The renter may apply to VCAT if the rental provider does not make the repairs within 14 days even without a repairs inspection and report.

Repairs in rental properties

## Rules when the renter is at fault

A rental provider can tell a renter to make or pay for repairs if they caused the damage or fault.

They must give the renter a ‘repair notice’. This is a written notice that says:

- what the damage is
- that the damage was caused by the renter
- whether they want the renter to repair the damage, or whether the rental provider will repair it.

If the renter is to organise the repair this must be done within 14 days and to the standard a tradesperson would make it. If they don’t do this, the rental provider may organise the repair at the renter’s expense.

If the rental provider is to organise the repair, they may ask the renter to cover the reasonable cost of repairs. Reasonable costs means costs that most people would think are fair. The law doesn’t define exactly what reasonable costs are, so if people can’t agree what is reasonable, they can apply to RDRV to help reach an agreement.

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT.

Repairs in rental properties

## Efficient replacements

If any water, gas or electricity appliances, fittings or fixtures need to be replaced, the rental provider must replace them with items that meet the minimum efficiency standards.

Repairs in rental properties

## Resolving disputes and issues

Try to resolve disputes by negotiating with the other person. If the renter cannot reach an agreement, there are formal ways to resolve disputes depending on your situation.

Repairs in rental properties

### Repairs inspection

One of our inspectors can visit the property and write a report about the repairs. This is a free service.

Renters can ask us for a repairs inspection if:

- the renter and rental provider cannot agree on who is at fault for a non-urgent repair
- the rental provider has ignored a request for non-urgent repairs to be made
- the renter wants us to investigate whether the rental provider has failed to ensure the property is maintained properly

Renters can ask us to do a repairs inspection by using the Request for repairs inspection or rent assessment (Word, 115KB) form. The renter must include the written notice sent to the rental provider with the form.

Consumer Affairs Victoria will send both the renter and the rental provider a copy of the report.

Repairs in rental properties

### Applying to RDRV

RDRV is a free alternative dispute resolution service offered by VCAT.

It’s available to renters, rental providers and estate agents to resolve disputes about many renting issues, including rent increases, repairs and bonds.

The renter can contact RDRV by phone, online or in person at any VCAT office.

Each application is case managed by a skilled resolution coordinator. They’ll liaise between renter and their rental provider to try to achieve a resolution at the earliest possible point.

A range of alternative dispute resolution methods may be used, including facilitated discussions and mediation.

For more information, visit Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria.

Repairs in rental properties

### Applying to VCAT

If the dispute is not resolved by RDRV, they can help the renter apply to VCAT.

Renters can apply to RDRV or VCAT if a rental provider:

- has not made an urgent repair
- has not repaid them for an urgent repair the renter organised and paid for because the rental provider did not respond to their request
- has ignored a repairs inspection report that says they must make a repair

Rental providers can apply to RDRV or VCAT if the renter:

- has not paid the rental provider back for a repair that was the renter’s fault

Repairs in rental properties

## Rental providers and tradespeople entering the property

Making repairs is one of the reasons a rental provider or agent can enter a rental property. They also have the right to bring someone to make the repairs.

They must give the renter at least 24 hours notice. They can only enter the property between 8am and 6pm on any day except a public holiday.

However, for an urgent repair, a renter might agree to let them enter at different times or with less notice.

Read more about rental providers entering a property.

Repairs in rental properties

### Requesting repairs or reimbursement

To request a non-urgent repair or reimbursement for urgent repairs, use one of these forms:

- Renters: Notice to rental provider of rented premises (Word, 97KB)
- Caravan park residents: Notice to owner of caravan or caravan park (Word, 743KB)
- Rooming house residents: Notice to operator of rooming house (Word, 734KB)

Repairs in rental properties

### Getting help from Consumer Affairs Victoria

To get help from Consumer Affairs Victoria, use one of these forms:

- Request for repairs inspection or rent assessment (Word, 115KB)
- Online enquiries form

Repairs in rental properties

### Urgent repairs guidelines

Consumer Affairs Victoria has guidelines that clarify the timeframes for responding to urgent repairs:

- Guideline 4 – Urgent repairs (Word, 297KB)

Repairs in rental properties

## Relevant legislation

If the renter want to know what the law says about urgent and non-urgent repairs, the renter can read these sections of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997:

- Section 72 – Urgent repair
- Section 74 – Application to Director to investigate need for non-urgent repairs
- Section 75 – Application to Tribunal for non-urgent repairs.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

# Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

A rental agreement is a contract between a renter and a rental provider. There is no cooling-off period after the renter signs the agreement. Renters should therefore understand the agreement before signing it.

Related information is available about:

- Applying for a rental property
- Paying a bond
- Unlawful discrimination
- Rooming-house agreements
- Residency in a caravan park
- Signing a site agreement in a residential park or village

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Making sure the property meets minimum standards

A rental provider must ensure that the property meets Victoria’s 15 minimum rental standards:

- before advertising the property
- before the renter moves into the property.

Renters should inspect the property before signing a rental agreement.

If the property does not meet the minimum standards:

- the renter can end the rental agreement before moving in
- after moving in, the renter can request an urgent repair to bring the property up to the minimum standards.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Using the correct rental agreement

A prescribed form must be used when entering into a written rental agreement. A prescribed form is a form required by Victorian rental law.

Consumer Affairs Victoria recommends using its official rental agreement form. See residential rental agreements and official forms before signing an agreement.

A renter or rental provider can request that additional conditions be included in the agreement. For example, an agreement may contain a condition prohibiting smoking inside the property.

However, an additional condition is invalid if it is inconsistent with:

- the Residential Tenancies Act 1997
- the standard rental agreement.

For example, a rental provider cannot include a condition allowing them to inspect the property every month.

See the list of conditions prohibited in residential rental agreements.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Receiving notices and documents electronically

A renter and rental provider can agree to exchange notices and other documents electronically, usually by email. This agreement should be recorded in the rental agreement.

When agreeing to electronic communication:

- each party should provide an email address that they check regularly
- a renter can withdraw their consent at any time by notifying the rental provider
- withdrawing consent should preferably be done in writing
- either party must notify the other immediately if their email address changes.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Paying rent and fees

A renter must be offered at least one rent-payment method that does not require them to pay a fee. This could include:

- direct bank transfer
- direct debit.

A rental provider cannot ask for or accept more than one month’s rent in advance unless the weekly rent is more than $900.

See rent payments and rent in advance for further information.

A rental provider cannot charge a renter for:

- preparing the rental agreement
- providing one complete set of property keys to each renter named in the agreement.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Bond amounts

In most cases, a rental provider cannot request a bond greater than one month’s rent.

See bond amounts and payments for exceptions and additional requirements.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Before signing a rental agreement

Entering into an agreement to rent a property creates a residential rental agreement. It is a legal agreement that can take time to end, so renters should make sure the property is suitable before signing.

Before the agreement is signed, the rental provider must disclose:

- whether they intend to sell the property
- whether they have engaged an agent to sell the property or entered into a contract of sale
- whether a mortgagee is taking action to possess the property or has commenced proceedings to enforce a mortgage
- whether they own the property or otherwise have the legal right to rent it out
- whether electricity is supplied through an embedded electricity network
- whether, to the best of their knowledge, the property or common property was the location of a homicide within the previous five years
- whether the property meets the rental minimum standards
- whether they received a repair notice concerning structural mould or damp within the previous three years
- the date of the most recent electricity safety check
- the date of the most recent gas safety check
- whether any recommendations from electricity or gas safety checks remain outstanding
- whether the property is heritage listed
- whether, to the best of their knowledge, the property was used for trafficking or cultivating a drug of dependence within the previous five years
- whether, to the best of their knowledge, the property contains asbestos
- whether the property is affected by a building or planning application lodged with a relevant planning authority
- whether the property or common property is subject to an official notice, order, declaration, report or recommendation concerning building defects or safety
- whether there is a current domestic building-work dispute concerning the property under the *Domestic Building Contracts Act 1995*
- whether there is a current dispute affecting the property under Part 10 of the *Owners Corporations Act 2006*
- whether the property is subject to owners-corporation rules.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

### Embedded electricity network information

If the property receives electricity through an embedded network, the rental provider must disclose:

- the embedded network’s trading name
- the Australian Business Number of the network operator
- the operator’s contact details
- applicable electricity tariffs
- other applicable fees
- where the renter can access this information, if it is not supplied directly.

### Building and safety notices

If an official notice, order, declaration, report or recommendation applies to the property, the rental provider must provide a description of it.

If owners-corporation rules apply, the rental provider must attach those rules to the rental application form.

## Terms that cannot be included in a rental agreement

A renter or rental provider can request additional terms and conditions. However, prohibited terms are invalid and cannot be enforced.

A rental provider who includes a prohibited term may face penalties.

See conditions that cannot be included in a residential rental agreement.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## What rental providers must give renters

At the start of every rental agreement, the rental provider or agent must give the renter:

- a copy of the written rental agreement
- a paper copy of the Renters guide, or a digital copy if the renter agreed to receive documents electronically
- a telephone number for arranging urgent repairs outside business hours
- the rental provider’s or agent’s full name
- a postal address for sending notices and documents
- an email address if electronic delivery of notices and documents was agreed to in writing
- one set of keys for every renter who signed the agreement
- two paper copies of the condition report, or one electronic copy.

If a bond is payable, the rental provider must also give the renter a bond-lodgement form so the bond can be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority.

If an owners corporation applies to the property, the renter must also receive a copy of its rules.

Knowing your rights when signing a rental agreement

## Checklist for signing a rental agreement

Before signing, the renter should confirm that:

- the agreement is complete and does not contain blank sections
- the bond is no more than one month’s rent, unless the weekly rent is more than $900
- they are not required to pay more than one month’s rent in advance, unless the weekly rent is more than $900 and they choose to do so
- at least one fee-free method of paying rent is available, excluding fees charged by the renter’s own bank
- any requested additional conditions have been discussed and recorded in the agreement
- they have not been charged for preparing the rental agreement.

An additional condition could, for example, require the rental provider to replace an oven within six months.

The renter should also review and agree to any negotiable terms concerning:

- pets
- cleaning
- gardening, mowing or general maintenance
- alterations or other changes to the property.
